questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

options.text: A balance sheet is prepared at a particular point of time and not for a particular period.
options.html: A balance sheet is prepared at a particular point of time and not for a particular period.

options.text: Those assets which cannot be seen or touched and have no volume but have value are called tangible assets.
options.html: Those assets which cannot be seen or touched and have no volume but have value are called tangible assets.

options.text: A balance sheet is a summary of balances of those ledger accounts which have not been closed by transfer to the trading account and the profit and loss account.
options.html: A balance sheet is a summary of balances of those ledger accounts which have not been closed by transfer to the trading account and the profit and loss account.

options.text: A balance sheet shows the nature and the value of assets and the nature and the amount of liabilities at a given date.
options.html: A balance sheet shows the nature and the value of assets and the nature and the amount of liabilities at a given date.

questions.solution:
The incorrect statement is Those assets which cannot be seen or touched and have no volume but have value are called tangible assets. 

Key Points

  • Those assets which cannot be seen or touched and have no volume but have value are called tangible assets:
    • This statement is incorrect. Assets that cannot be seen or touched and have no physical presence but have value are called intangible assets, not tangible assets.
    • Intangible assets include intellectual property, goodwill, patents, trademarks, and copyrights.
    • Tangible assets, on the other hand, are physical assets that can be seen and touched, such as machinery, buildings, and inventory.

Additional Information

  • A balance sheet is prepared at a particular point of time and not for a particular period:
    • This is correct. A balance sheet provides a snapshot of a company's financial position at a specific point in time, showing the assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity.
  • A balance sheet is a summary of balances of those ledger accounts which have not been closed by transfer to the trading account and the profit and loss account:
    • This is correct. The balance sheet summarizes the remaining balances after the revenue and expense accounts have been closed to the trading and profit and loss accounts.
  • A balance sheet shows the nature and the value of assets and the nature and the amount of liabilities at a given date:
    • This is correct. The balance sheet details the types and values of a company's assets and liabilities at a specific date, providing insight into the company's financial stability.

questions.question: Which of the following items is NOT recorded in profit and loss account ?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following items is NOT recorded in profit and loss account ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Return outward is not recorded in the profit and loss account.

Key Points

  • Return outward:
    • Return outward, also known as purchase returns, refers to goods that a business returns to its suppliers. This transaction is recorded in the purchase returns account and is deducted from total purchases in the trading account, not in the profit and loss account.
    • It impacts the cost of goods sold (COGS) calculation but does not directly affect the profit and loss account.

Additional Information

  • Administrative expenses:
    • These are overhead costs related to the general operation of a business, such as salaries of office staff, rent, utilities, and office supplies. They are recorded in the profit and loss account as they directly affect the net profit of the business.
  • Depreciation of office assets:
    • Depreciation represents the reduction in value of office assets over time due to wear and tear, age, or obsolescence. It is recorded as an expense in the profit and loss account to reflect the cost of using long-term assets.
  • Profit on sale of assets:
    • When a business sells an asset and makes a profit, this profit is recorded in the profit and loss account. It is part of other incomes or gains and contributes to the overall profitability of the business.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Book - debts are recorded in the credit column of the trial balance.
options.html: Book - debts are recorded in the credit column of the trial balance.

options.text: Cash in hand is recorded in the credit column of the trial balance.
options.html: Cash in hand is recorded in the credit column of the trial balance.

options.text: The trial balance contains balances of only personal and real accounts.
options.html: The trial balance contains balances of only personal and real accounts.

options.text: The balance of the liabilities account is shown in the credit column of the trial balance.
options.html: The balance of the liabilities account is shown in the credit column of the trial balance.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is The balance of the liabilities account is shown in the credit column of the trial balance.

Key Points

  • The balance of the liabilities account is shown in the credit column of the trial balance:
    • In accounting, liabilities represent the financial obligations of a business. These are amounts the business owes to external parties, such as loans, accounts payable, and other debts.
    • Liabilities are recorded on the credit side of the trial balance because they represent amounts that the business needs to pay in the future.
    • The trial balance is a statement that lists the balances of all ledger accounts. It helps ensure that the total debits equal the total credits, maintaining the accounting equation.
    • By showing liabilities in the credit column, the trial balance accurately reflects the financial position of the business.

Additional Information

  • Book-debts are recorded in the credit column of the trial balance:
    • This is incorrect. Book-debts, or accounts receivable, represent amounts owed to the business by its customers. These are assets and are recorded in the debit column of the trial balance.
  • Cash in hand is recorded in the credit column of the trial balance:
    • Incorrect. Cash in hand is an asset and is recorded in the debit column of the trial balance.
  • The trial balance contains balances of only personal and real accounts:
    • This statement is incorrect. The trial balance contains balances of all types of accounts, including personal, real, and nominal accounts.

questions.question: Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements? Statement - 1 : Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is to be followed by companies so that investors have an optimum level of consistency in the financial statements they use when analysing companies for investment purposes. Statement - 2 : Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) cover aspects like revenue recognition, balance sheet item classification and outstanding share measurements.
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements?

Statement - 1 : Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is to be followed by companies so that investors have an optimum level of consistency in the financial statements they use when analysing companies for investment purposes.

Statement - 2 : Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) cover aspects like revenue recognition, balance sheet item classification and outstanding share measurements.

options.text: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are correct
options.html: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are correct

options.text: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are incorrect
options.html: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are incorrect

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are correct.

Key Points

  • Statement - 1: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) is to be followed by companies so that investors have an optimum level of consistency in the financial statements they use when analysing companies for investment purposes:
    • GAAP ensures that companies use standardized accounting methods and principles, which provides consistency and comparability across financial statements.
    • This consistency is crucial for investors as it allows them to compare financial performance and make informed investment decisions.
    • Without GAAP, financial statements could vary widely in terms of presentation and accounting methods, making it difficult to evaluate the financial health and performance of different companies.
  • Statement - 2: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) cover aspects like revenue recognition, balance sheet item classification and outstanding share measurements:
    • GAAP encompasses a wide range of accounting practices, including how and when revenue is recognized, how different items are classified on the balance sheet, and how shares outstanding are measured and reported.
    • These principles ensure that financial statements are accurate, consistent, and reliable, which is essential for stakeholders such as investors, creditors, and regulators.
    • By covering these aspects, GAAP helps maintain transparency and trust in the financial reporting process.

Additional Information

  • Only statement - 2 is correct:
    • This option is incorrect because both statements are accurate. Statement - 1 correctly explains the importance of GAAP for consistency in financial statements, and Statement - 2 accurately describes the scope of GAAP.
  • Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are incorrect:
    • This option is incorrect as both statements are correct. GAAP provides consistency in financial reporting (Statement - 1) and covers various accounting aspects (Statement - 2).
  • Only statement - 1 is correct:
    • This option is incorrect because Statement - 2 is also correct. GAAP does cover aspects like revenue recognition, balance sheet item classification, and outstanding share measurements.

questions.question: In relation to limitations of financial accounting, which of the following statements is INCORRECT ?
questions.questionHtml: In relation to limitations of financial accounting, which of the following statements is INCORRECT ?

options.text: Financial accounting discloses the present value of the business.
options.html: Financial accounting discloses the present value of the business.

options.text: Financial accounting is influenced by personal judgements.
options.html: Financial accounting is influenced by personal judgements.

options.text: Financial accounting ignores important non-monetary information.
options.html: Financial accounting ignores important non-monetary information.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Financial accounting discloses the present value of the business.

Key Points

  • Financial accounting discloses the present value of the business:
    • This statement is incorrect because financial accounting typically records assets and liabilities at their historical cost rather than their current or fair market value.
    • Historical cost accounting does not reflect the present value of the business, which may be significantly different due to market fluctuations, inflation, or changes in the business environment.
    • To ascertain the present value of the business, other valuation methods such as discounted cash flow analysis or market value assessments are required.
  • Financial accounting permits alternative treatments:
    • This statement is correct. Financial accounting often allows for alternative methods of recording and reporting financial transactions, such as different inventory valuation methods (FIFO, LIFO, Weighted Average) or depreciation methods (Straight Line, Declining Balance).
    • These alternatives can lead to variations in financial results and comparisons between companies, making it difficult to achieve uniformity and comparability.
  • Financial accounting is influenced by personal judgements:
    • This statement is correct. Financial accounting requires the use of estimates and judgements, such as in the valuation of assets, determination of useful lives for depreciation, and estimation of bad debts.
    • These subjective judgements can introduce bias and affect the reliability and objectivity of financial statements.
  • Financial accounting ignores important non-monetary information:
    • This statement is correct. Financial accounting primarily focuses on monetary transactions and does not capture qualitative factors such as employee skills, customer satisfaction, or brand reputation.
    • These non-monetary elements can be crucial for a comprehensive understanding of a business's performance and potential but are not reflected in financial statements.

Additional Information

  • Financial accounting is not designed to measure business performance:
    • While financial accounting provides valuable financial information, it is not solely designed to measure business performance comprehensively. Performance measurement often requires additional tools and metrics, such as balanced scorecards or performance dashboards, to capture both financial and non-financial indicators.
  • Financial accounting is primarily for external reporting:
    • Financial accounting is intended to provide information to external stakeholders such as investors, creditors, and regulatory bodies, rather than for internal management purposes. For internal decision-making, management accounting and other internal reporting tools are more appropriate.
  • Financial accounting follows GAAP or IFRS:
    • Financial accounting adheres to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) or International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), ensuring consistency, reliability, and comparability of financial information across different entities.
  • Financial accounting focuses on historical data:
    • Financial accounting primarily records past transactions and events, providing a historical view of the business's financial performance and position. It does not typically focus on forward-looking information or future projections.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The income and expenditure account is a real account.
options.html: The income and expenditure account is a real account.

options.text: The receipts and payments account is a summary of all the capital receipts and payments.
options.html: The receipts and payments account is a summary of all the capital receipts and payments.

options.text: Income and expenditure relating to special funds should not be dealt with in the income and expenditure account.
options.html: Income and expenditure relating to special funds should not be dealt with in the income and expenditure account.

options.text: Payment of honorarium is treated as a capital expenditure.
options.html: Payment of honorarium is treated as a capital expenditure.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Income and expenditure relating to special funds should not be dealt with in the income and expenditure account.

Key Points

  • Income and expenditure relating to special funds should not be dealt with in the income and expenditure account:
    • Special funds are designated for specific purposes and are separate from the general income and expenditure of an organization.
    • Examples include endowment funds, building funds, and scholarship funds.
    • Transactions related to these funds are recorded in separate accounts to ensure they are used for their intended purposes.
    • By keeping these transactions separate, organizations maintain financial transparency and accountability.

Additional Information

  • The income and expenditure account is a real account:
    • This statement is incorrect. The income and expenditure account is a nominal account, not a real account. It records revenue and expenses over a specific period and determines the surplus or deficit.
  • The receipts and payments account is a summary of all the capital receipts and payments:
    • This statement is incorrect. The receipts and payments account is a summary of all cash transactions, both capital and revenue, over a specific period. It does not exclusively summarize capital receipts and payments.
  • Payment of honorarium is treated as a capital expenditure:
    • This statement is incorrect. Payment of honorarium is treated as a revenue expenditure. It is a payment for services rendered and is recorded as an expense in the income and expenditure account.

questions.question: When starting balance is debit, i.e., favourable balance as per cash book, identify which of the following transactions will be added ?
questions.questionHtml: When starting balance is debit, i.e., favourable balance as per cash book, identify which of the following transactions will be added ?

options.text: Wrong credit granted by the bank
options.html: Wrong credit granted by the bank

options.text: Direct payment by the bank as per standing instruction
options.html: Direct payment by the bank as per standing instruction

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Wrong credit granted by the bank.

Key Points

  • Wrong credit granted by the bank:
    • This transaction involves the bank erroneously crediting an amount to the company's account, increasing the balance in the cash book.
    • Since the starting balance is a debit (favourable balance), this wrong credit will be added to reconcile the balance as per the cash book with the bank statement.
    • This adjustment is necessary to reflect the true balance after accounting for the bank's error.

Additional Information

  • Cheque recorded but not deposited:
    • This would not be added but subtracted. If a cheque is recorded in the cash book but not deposited in the bank, it means the cash book shows more balance than the bank statement.
  • Bill of exchange dishonoured:
    • This would be subtracted. If a bill of exchange is dishonoured, it means the expected payment was not received, reducing the balance in the cash book.
  • Direct payment by the bank as per standing instruction:
    • This would be subtracted. Direct payments by the bank, such as standing instructions for utility bills, would reduce the balance in the bank statement but may not immediately be reflected in the cash book.

questions.question: _______ is defined as a statement or a list of all ledger account balances taken from various ledger books on a particular date to check the arithmetical accuracy.
questions.questionHtml: _______ is defined as a statement or a list of all ledger account balances taken from various ledger books on a particular date to check the arithmetical accuracy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Trial balance is defined as a statement or a list of all ledger account balances taken from various ledger books on a particular date to check the arithmetical accuracy.

Key Points

  • Trial balance is defined as a statement or a list of all ledger account balances taken from various ledger books on a particular date to check the arithmetical accuracy:
    • A trial balance is prepared to verify the equality of debit and credit balances in the ledger accounts.
    • It is an essential tool for accountants to ensure that the bookkeeping entries are mathematically correct.
    • The trial balance helps in identifying any discrepancies or errors in the ledger entries before the preparation of financial statements.
    • It is usually prepared at the end of an accounting period to assist in the preparation of the final accounts.

Additional Information

  • Pass book:
    • A pass book is a record provided by a bank to its account holders detailing all transactions in their account. It is not used to check the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts.
  • Compound posting:
    • Compound posting refers to the accounting practice of recording a single transaction that affects multiple accounts, typically involving both debits and credits. It is a method of recording transactions, not a tool for verifying ledger accuracy.
  • General journal:
    • The general journal is a book of original entry where all accounting transactions are first recorded. While it is crucial for maintaining an accurate record of transactions, it is not specifically used to check the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT in relation to Non - Profit Organisations Accounts?

options.text: Receipt and Payment Account follows Nominal Account rules.
options.html: Receipt and Payment Account follows Nominal Account rules.

options.text: Receipt and Payment Account is similar to cash book.
options.html: Receipt and Payment Account is similar to cash book.

options.text: All cash payments both capital and revenue during the period are credited to Receipt and Payment Account.
options.html: All cash payments both capital and revenue during the period are credited to Receipt and Payment Account.

options.text: No provisions are recorded in Receipt and Payment Account.
options.html: No provisions are recorded in Receipt and Payment Account.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Receipt and Payment Account follows Nominal Account rules.

Key Points

  • Receipt and Payment Account follows Nominal Account rules:
    • This statement is incorrect. The Receipt and Payment Account is a real account, not a nominal account. It records all cash and bank transactions related to receipts and payments, regardless of their nature (capital or revenue).
    • Nominal accounts, on the other hand, deal with incomes, expenses, gains, and losses, which are not directly recorded in the Receipt and Payment Account.

Additional Information

  • Receipt and Payment Account is similar to cash book:
    • This statement is correct. The Receipt and Payment Account is similar to a cash book as it records all cash and bank transactions during an accounting period. It shows the opening balance, receipts, payments, and closing balance of cash and bank accounts.
  • All cash payments both capital and revenue during the period are credited to Receipt and Payment Account:
    • This statement is correct. The Receipt and Payment Account captures all cash payments made during the period, whether they are of a capital or revenue nature, on the credit side.
  • No provisions are recorded in Receipt and Payment Account:
    • This statement is correct. Provisions, which are non-cash items, are not recorded in the Receipt and Payment Account. This account only captures actual cash and bank transactions.

questions.question: Valuing inventory at cost or net realisable value is based on which principle ?
questions.questionHtml: Valuing inventory at cost or net realisable value is based on which principle ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Conservatism.

Key Points

  • Conservatism:
    • The principle of conservatism in accounting advises that potential expenses and liabilities should be recognized immediately, but revenues should only be recognized when they are assured.
    • Valuing inventory at the lower of cost or net realizable value ensures that an entity does not overstate its financial position by recognizing inventory at an amount greater than what can be realized from its sale.
    • This approach prevents the overstatement of assets and income, aligning with the conservative principle of "anticipate no profits but anticipate all losses."

Additional Information

  • Going Concern:
    • This principle assumes that a business will continue to operate indefinitely and not go bankrupt or be liquidated in the near future.
    • While important, it does not directly relate to the valuation of inventory.
  • Consistency:
    • This principle states that a company should use the same accounting methods and procedures from period to period unless a change is justified.
    • It ensures comparability over time but does not specifically address how inventory should be valued.
  • Historical Cost:
    • This principle states that assets should be recorded and reported at their original purchase cost.
    • While inventory may initially be recorded at historical cost, the conservatism principle requires it to be written down if the net realizable value is lower.

questions.question: Which of the following items is recorded in profit and loss appropriation account ?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following items is recorded in profit and loss appropriation account ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Transfer to general reserve.

Key Points

  • Transfer to general reserve:
    • The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is used to allocate the net profit of a company to various reserves and provisions. One of the key allocations made from this account is the transfer to the General Reserve.
    • The General Reserve is an amount set aside from profits to strengthen the financial position of the company and to meet future contingencies or liabilities.
    • This transfer is a key component of profit appropriation and is recorded in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.

Additional Information

  • Bad debts:
    • This is an expense that arises when a company is unable to collect money owed by its debtors. It is recorded in the Profit and Loss Account, not in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
  • Accrued interest:
    • This represents interest that has been incurred but not yet paid. It is recorded in the Profit and Loss Account as an expense or income, depending on whether the company is the borrower or lender, respectively.
  • Printing and stationery:
    • This is an operational expense related to office supplies. It is recorded in the Profit and Loss Account as an expense.

questions.question: In India, the _______ governs the provisions for bills of exchange.
questions.questionHtml: In India, the _______ governs the provisions for bills of exchange.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

Key Points

  • Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881:
    • This Act specifically deals with negotiable instruments such as bills of exchange, promissory notes, and cheques.
    • It lays down the legal framework for the creation, transfer, and enforcement of these instruments.
    • The Act ensures that the holder of such instruments has a clear legal right to recover the amount due.

Additional Information

  • Companies Act, 2013:
    • This Act primarily governs the incorporation, regulation, and dissolution of companies in India.
    • It does not deal with the provisions for bills of exchange, which are covered under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
  • Partnership Act, 1932:
    • This Act governs the formation, operation, and dissolution of partnerships in India.
    • It does not address the legal framework for negotiable instruments like bills of exchange.
  • Income Tax Act, 1961:
    • This Act deals with the taxation of income in India.
    • It does not cover the provisions for negotiable instruments such as bills of exchange.

questions.question: Income Statement of a charitable institution is known as:
questions.questionHtml: Income Statement of a charitable institution is known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer isIncome and Expenditure A/c.

Key Points

  • Income and Expenditure A/c:
    • It is a summary of all income earned and expenses incurred by a charitable institution during a specific period, usually a financial year.
    • This account reflects the operating results of the institution, showing whether it has a surplus or deficit.
    • It is similar to the Profit and Loss A/c used by for-profit businesses but adapted for non-profit organizations.

Additional Information

  • Receipts and Payments A/c:
    • This is a cash-based summary of all receipts and payments made during a financial period. It does not consider accruals and thus does not show the financial performance accurately.
  • Profit and Loss A/c:
    • This account is used by for-profit businesses to show the profitability over a period. Charitable institutions use the Income and Expenditure A/c instead.
  • Statement of Affairs:
    • This is a statement showing the financial position of an organization, including its assets and liabilities. It is not used to reflect the income and expenditure of a period.

questions.question: Sunil owed Rohit Rs. 80,000. Rohit draws a bill on Sunil for that amount for 3 months on 1 April 2015. Sunil accepts it and returns it to Rohit. On 15 April 2015, Rohit discounts it with HFDC Bank at a discount of 12% p.a. What is the amount of discount?
questions.questionHtml: Sunil owed Rohit Rs. 80,000. Rohit draws a bill on Sunil for that amount for 3 months on 1 April 2015. Sunil accepts it and returns it to Rohit. On 15 April 2015, Rohit discounts it with HFDC Bank at a discount of 12% p.a. What is the amount of discount?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is - ₹2,000

Key Points

  • Bill Amount: ₹80,000
  • Bill Date: 1 April 2015
  • Term: 3 months → Due date = 1 July 2015
  • Discounting Date: 15 April 2015
  • Discount Rate: 12% per annum
  • Discounting Period:
    • From 15 April to 1 July = 77 days
  • Discount Calculation:
    • Formula: Discount = (Amount × Rate × Time) / (100 × 365)
    • = (80,000 × 12 × 77) / (100 × 365) = ₹2,021.37 ≈ ₹2,000

Additional Information

  • Bill of Exchange
    • A negotiable instrument where one party (drawer) orders another (drawee) to pay a fixed sum.
    • When accepted by the drawee, it becomes a legal liability to pay on the due date.
  • Discounting of Bills
    • The bill is sold to a bank before maturity for a price less than its face value.
    • The difference between the bill amount and the amount received is called the discount.
  • Time and Due Dates
    • For calculation of maturity, 3 days of grace are generally added (unless stated otherwise).
    • In this case, 1 April + 3 months = 1 July (due date), no grace days are mentioned as it is implied in modern banking.

questions.question: Which of the following are regarded as features of the single - entry system, generally maintained by small shopkeepers? (i) Maintenance of transactions related to personal accounts on the double entry basis and maintenance of transactions related to real and nominal accounts on the single entry basis. (ii) Maintenance of a cash book with mixed transactions. Normally, both personal and business transactions are mixed in a cash book. (iii) Form and accounting accuracy of the single-entry system differ from firm to firm
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following are regarded as features of the single - entry system, generally maintained by small shopkeepers?

(i) Maintenance of transactions related to personal accounts on the double entry basis and maintenance of transactions related to real and nominal accounts on the single entry basis.

(ii) Maintenance of a cash book with mixed transactions. Normally, both personal and business transactions are mixed in a cash book.

(iii) Form and accounting accuracy of the single-entry system differ from firm to firm
questions.solution:
The correct answer is All of (i), (ii), and (iii).

Key Points

  • Maintenance of transactions related to personal accounts on the double entry basis and maintenance of transactions related to real and nominal accounts on the single entry basis:
    • This is a key feature of the single-entry system. Personal accounts are often maintained using the double-entry system to ensure accuracy in personal dealings, while real and nominal accounts may use the single-entry system, which is simpler and less time-consuming.
  • Maintenance of a cash book with mixed transactions:
    • In a single-entry system, small shopkeepers often maintain a cash book where both personal and business transactions are recorded together. This mixed recording is typical of the less formal accounting practices seen in small businesses.
  • Form and accounting accuracy of the single-entry system differ from firm to firm:
    • The single-entry system lacks standardization, meaning that each firm may implement it differently. This variability can lead to differences in accounting accuracy and the overall form of the records kept.

Additional Information

  • Only (i) and (iii):
    • While (i) and (iii) are correct features of the single-entry system, this option overlooks the importance of maintaining a cash book with mixed transactions, which is also a significant characteristic.
  • Only (i) and (ii):
    • This option is incomplete as it misses out on the fact that the form and accuracy of the single-entry system can vary from firm to firm, which is a notable feature of this system.
  • Only (ii) and (iii):
    • Although (ii) and (iii) are correct, this option fails to acknowledge that personal accounts are often maintained on a double-entry basis while real and nominal accounts are on a single-entry basis, which is a crucial aspect of the single-entry system.

questions.question: _______ is often referred to as book of prime entry or the book of original entry.
questions.questionHtml: _______ is often referred to as book of prime entry or the book of original entry.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Journal.

Key Points

  • Journal is often referred to as book of prime entry or the book of original entry:
    • The journal is the initial record where all financial transactions are first entered before they are posted to the ledger accounts. This is why it is called the book of original entry or prime entry.
    • It captures the chronological sequence of transactions, ensuring that no transaction is overlooked or omitted.
    • The journal includes details such as the date of the transaction, accounts affected, amounts, and a brief description, providing a comprehensive record of all business activities.

Additional Information

  • Book-keeping:
    • Book-keeping refers to the process of recording financial transactions systematically. While it involves the use of journals and ledgers, it is not specifically the book of original entry.
  • Ledger:
    • The ledger is a book or a collection of accounts where transactions from the journal are posted and categorized. It is not the first place of entry but rather a place for organizing and summarizing financial data.
  • Capital book:
    • The capital book is not a standard term in accounting. It might refer to records related to capital accounts, but it is not the book of original entry.

questions.question: _______ convention underlines the prudence of under-stating than over - stating the net income of an entity for a period and the net assets as on a particular date.
questions.questionHtml: _______ convention underlines the prudence of under-stating than over - stating the net income of an entity for a period and the net assets as on a particular date.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Conservatism.

Key Points

  • Conservatism convention:
    • The conservatism convention, also known as the prudence concept, is a key accounting principle that guides accountants to exercise caution and opt for solutions that will result in lower profits and asset valuations. This approach ensures that the financial statements do not overstate the financial health of the entity.
    • Under this convention, potential losses are recorded as soon as they are anticipated, while gains are only recognized when they are realized.
    • This principle helps in providing a more realistic view of an entity's financial position, protecting stakeholders from over-optimistic projections that could lead to financial mismanagement or fraud.

Additional Information

  • Materiality:
    • This concept focuses on the significance of transactions, balances, and errors in financial statements. Information is considered material if its omission or misstatement could influence the economic decisions of users. It does not specifically address the prudence of under-stating net income or assets.
  • Historical cost:
    • Historical cost principle requires that assets be recorded at their original purchase price. This principle does not deal with the prudence of under-stating or over-stating net income or assets but rather emphasizes recording assets at the cost at which they were acquired.
  • Consistency:
    • The consistency principle states that companies should use the same accounting methods and procedures from period to period unless a change is justified. This principle ensures comparability of financial statements over time but does not directly relate to the prudence of under-stating net income or assets.

questions.question: Accounting is rightly referred to as the '_______ of business'.
questions.questionHtml: Accounting is rightly referred to as the '_______ of business'.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is language.

Key Points

  • Language of Business:
    • Accounting is often referred to as the "language of business" because it is the medium through which financial information is communicated to stakeholders.
    • It provides a systematic way of recording, reporting, and analyzing financial transactions, which is essential for decision-making within a business.
    • Through financial statements, accounting conveys the economic activities and conditions of a business to managers, investors, regulators, and other stakeholders.
    • This helps in understanding the financial health and performance of a business, thereby facilitating informed decision-making.

Additional Information

  • Vision:
    • Vision refers to the long-term goals and aspirations of a business. It is a forward-looking statement that outlines what the business aims to achieve in the future.
    • While important for strategic direction, vision is not a term that captures the essence of accounting's role in business communication.
  • Perception:
    • Perception relates to the way stakeholders view or understand the business, which can be influenced by branding, public relations, and marketing.
    • Perception is subjective and does not directly relate to the systematic and objective nature of accounting.
  • Mission:
    • Mission defines the core purpose and values of a business. It is a statement that articulates what the business does, for whom, and why.
    • While the mission is crucial for guiding business operations, it does not encapsulate the communicative function of accounting.

questions.question: Which of the following methods of depreciation is prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following methods of depreciation is prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Written-down value method.

Key Points

  • Written-down value method:
    • This method is prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961 for calculating depreciation for tax purposes.
    • In the written-down value (WDV) method, depreciation is calculated on the book value of the asset, which reduces each year. This results in higher depreciation expenses in the initial years and lower expenses in the later years.
    • This method aligns with the principle of matching expenses with revenues, as assets are typically more productive in their earlier years.

Additional Information

  • Sum-of-years-digits method:
    • This method accelerates depreciation, similar to the written-down value method, but is not prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961.
    • Depreciation is calculated by multiplying the depreciable amount by a fraction, which decreases each year. This method is more complex and less commonly used for tax purposes.
  • Production hour method:
    • This method calculates depreciation based on the actual usage or production hours of the asset, making it suitable for machinery and equipment.
    • However, it is not prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961 for calculating tax depreciation.
  • Double-declining balance method:
    • This is another accelerated depreciation method where depreciation is calculated at double the rate of the straight-line method.
    • Although it provides higher depreciation expenses in the early years, it is not prescribed by the Income Tax Act, 1961 for tax purposes.

  • Freight and insurance paid for acquiring goods:

    • Debiting these expenses to the trading account aligns with the matching principle in accounting, which states that expenses should be matched with the revenues they help to generate.
    • The trading account is used to calculate the gross profit or loss by comparing the cost of goods sold with sales revenue.

Additional Information

  • Credited to the profit and loss account:
    • This is incorrect because profit and loss accounts are used for recording revenues and expenses that are not directly related to the cost of goods sold. Freight and insurance are directly related to the cost of goods sold.
  • Debited to the profit and loss account:

  • Credited to the trading account:
    • This is incorrect because the trading account is debited for costs that are incurred to bring goods to a saleable condition, not credited.

questions.question: "Each transaction is analysed into the debit aspect and the credit aspect. This helps to find out how each transaction will financially affect the business". The given statement is regarded as which function of journal?
questions.questionHtml:
"Each transaction is analysed into the debit aspect and the credit aspect. This helps to find out how each transaction will financially affect the business".

The given statement is regarded as which function of journal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Analytical function.

Key Points

  • Analytical function:
    • The analytical function of a journal involves breaking down each transaction into its debit and credit components.
    • This process helps in understanding how each transaction affects the financial position of the business.
    • By analyzing the debit and credit aspects, businesses can ensure that their financial records are accurate and balanced.
    • This function is crucial for maintaining the integrity of financial data and for subsequent financial reporting and analysis.

Additional Information

  • Historical function:
    • This function involves recording transactions in chronological order. It serves as a historical record of all business transactions, but it does not emphasize the analysis of transactions.
  • Recording function:
    • The recording function pertains to the initial documentation of transactions in the journal. While it is essential, it focuses more on the entry of data rather than the analysis.
  • Secondary function:
    • This is a broad term that can refer to additional functions of the journal, such as providing a basis for future reference, but it does not specifically address the analytical aspect of transactions.

questions.question: ________ convention proposes that while accounting for various transactions, only those which may have significant effect on profitability or financial status of the business should have special consideration for reporting.
questions.questionHtml: ________ convention proposes that while accounting for various transactions, only those which may have significant effect on profitability or financial status of the business should have special consideration for reporting.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Materiality.

Key Points

  • Materiality convention proposes that while accounting for various transactions, only those which may have significant effect on profitability or financial status of the business should have special consideration for reporting:
    • The materiality principle in accounting suggests that all significant information that could influence the decision of a user of financial statements should be disclosed.
    • Transactions or items are considered material if their omission or misstatement could influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of the financial statements.
    • This principle helps in focusing on the most relevant and impactful financial information, ensuring that users get a clear and accurate picture of the business's financial status.
    • Materiality is subjective and may vary depending on the size and nature of the business and the specific circumstances of the transaction.

Additional Information

  • Consistency:
    • This principle states that companies should use the same accounting methods and procedures from period to period unless a change is justified and disclosed. It ensures comparability of financial statements over different periods but does not relate to the significance of transactions.
  • Historical cost:
    • This principle requires assets to be recorded at their original purchase cost. It does not consider the significance of transactions in terms of their effect on profitability or financial status.
  • Conservatism:
    • This principle advises that potential expenses and liabilities should be recognized as soon as possible, but revenue should only be recognized when it is assured. While it impacts the reporting of financial status, it does not specifically address the materiality of transactions.

questions.question: Which concept enables the accountant to carry forward the values of assets and liabilities from one accounting period to the other without asking the question about usefulness and worth of the assets and recoverability of the receivables?
questions.questionHtml: Which concept enables the accountant to carry forward the values of assets and liabilities from one accounting period to the other without asking the question about usefulness and worth of the assets and recoverability of the receivables?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Going Concern Concept.

Key Points

  • Going Concern Concept:
    • This concept assumes that a business will continue to operate indefinitely, and it will not be liquidated in the foreseeable future.
    • Because of this assumption, accountants can carry forward the values of assets and liabilities from one accounting period to the next without questioning their current usefulness or worth.
    • This enables the financial statements to be prepared on a historical cost basis rather than a liquidation basis, ensuring consistency and comparability over time.

Additional Information

  • Business Entity Concept:
    • This concept states that a business is a separate legal entity from its owners. All financial transactions of the business are recorded separately from the personal transactions of the owners.
    • While important, this concept does not address the continuation of asset and liability values across accounting periods.
  • Money Measurement Concept:
    • This concept states that only transactions that can be measured in monetary terms are recorded in the accounting books.
    • It does not address the continuation of asset and liability values from one period to another.
  • Accounting Period Concept:
    • This concept states that the life of a business is divided into specific periods (such as months, quarters, or years) for the purpose of financial reporting.
    • While it helps in preparing periodic financial statements, it does not address the ongoing valuation of assets and liabilities.

questions.question: ________ method is especially suited to mines, oil wells. quarries, sandpits and similar assets of a wasting character.
questions.questionHtml: ________ method is especially suited to mines, oil wells. quarries, sandpits and similar assets of a wasting character.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Depletion.

Key Points

  • Depletion method is especially suited to mines, oil wells, quarries, sandpits and similar assets of a wasting character:
    • Depletion refers to the allocation of the cost of natural resources over time as they are extracted and used.
    • This method is particularly relevant for industries involved in the extraction of natural resources, such as mining, oil drilling, and quarrying.
    • It ensures that the expense associated with the asset's usage is matched with the revenue generated from the sale of the extracted resources.
    • Depletion can be calculated using either the cost depletion method or the percentage depletion method.

Additional Information

  • Amortisation:
    • Amortisation is the process of spreading the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life.
    • It is typically applied to assets such as patents, trademarks, and goodwill.
    • Since mines, oil wells, and quarries are tangible assets, amortisation is not the appropriate method for these.
  • Depreciation:
    • Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life.
    • It is used for assets like machinery, buildings, and vehicles.
    • While similar to depletion, depreciation is not specifically designed for wasting natural resources.
  • Dilapidation:
    • Dilapidation refers to the state of disrepair or deterioration of a building or structure due to neglect or misuse.
    • It is not a method of cost allocation and thus is not relevant to the context of natural resource extraction.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are correct? Statement - 1 : In periods of rising prices, the cost of production is lower in case of the FIFO method. Statement - 2 : In periods of falling prices, the ending inventory is valued in the FIFO method at a price lower than that in case of the LIFO method.
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

Statement - 1 : In periods of rising prices, the cost of production is lower in case of the FIFO method.

Statement - 2 : In periods of falling prices, the ending inventory is valued in the FIFO method at a price lower than that in case of the LIFO method.

options.text: Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are incorrect.
options.html: Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are incorrect.

options.text: Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are correct.
options.html: Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are correct.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are correct.

Key Points

  • FIFO (First-In, First-Out) Method:
    • Under the FIFO method, the oldest inventory items are recorded as sold first. Therefore, in periods of rising prices, the cost of goods sold (COGS) is based on the lower cost of older inventory, resulting in a lower COGS and higher gross profit.
    • This results in a lower cost of production during periods of rising prices because the older, cheaper inventory is used up first.
  • LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) Method:
    • In contrast, under the LIFO method, the most recently acquired inventory is recorded as sold first. During periods of rising prices, this means the COGS will be higher, as it reflects the cost of the more expensive, newer inventory.

In periods of falling prices, the ending inventory is valued in the FIFO method at a price lower than that in case of the LIFO method.

Key Points

  • Ending Inventory Valuation in FIFO:
    • Under FIFO, the ending inventory is composed of the most recently purchased items. In periods of falling prices, these items are cheaper than the older inventory.
    • Therefore, the ending inventory in FIFO will be valued at a lower price compared to LIFO, where the ending inventory consists of older, more expensive items.
  • Ending Inventory Valuation in LIFO:
    • Under LIFO, the ending inventory is composed of the older, more expensive items in periods of falling prices. This results in a higher valuation compared to FIFO.

Additional Information

  • Only Statement - 2 is correct:
    • This is incorrect because both statements are correct. The FIFO method results in a lower cost of production in rising prices and a lower ending inventory value in falling prices.
  • Both Statement - 1 and Statement - 2 are incorrect:
    • This is incorrect as both statements are accurate reflections of the FIFO method's impact in different price scenarios.
  • Only Statement - 1 is correct:
    • This is incorrect as it ignores the accuracy of Statement 2. Both statements are correct.

Statement - 2 : Under Self Balancing Ledger system three ledger accounts are prepared, viz, General Ledger Adjustment Account, which is maintained under Debtors Ledger and Creditors Ledger and Debtors or Sales Ledger Adjustment Account and Creditors or Purchase Ledger Adjustments Accounts, which are maintained under General Ledger.

Which of the given options best describes the truthfulness of the following statements?

Statement - 1 : Under Self Balancing Ledger system each ledger is prepared under double entry system and a complete trial balance can also be prepared by taking up the balances of ledger accounts.

Statement - 2 : Under Self Balancing Ledger system three ledger accounts are prepared, viz, General Ledger Adjustment Account, which is maintained under Debtors Ledger and Creditors Ledger and Debtors or Sales Ledger Adjustment Account and Creditors or Purchase Ledger Adjustments Accounts, which are maintained under General Ledger.

options.html: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are incorrect

options.text: Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are correct

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are correct.

Key Points

  • Statement - 1: Under Self Balancing Ledger system each ledger is prepared under double entry system and a complete trial balance can also be prepared by taking up the balances of ledger accounts:
    • Under the Self Balancing Ledger system, each ledger (General Ledger, Debtors Ledger, and Creditors Ledger) is maintained using the double entry system.
    • This ensures that every transaction is recorded in two accounts, maintaining the accounting equation and allowing for a complete trial balance to be prepared.
    • Each ledger can provide a trial balance independently, which helps in detecting errors within that specific ledger.
  • Statement - 2: Under Self Balancing Ledger system three ledger accounts are prepared, viz, General Ledger Adjustment Account, which is maintained under Debtors Ledger and Creditors Ledger and Debtors or Sales Ledger Adjustment Account and Creditors or Purchase Ledger Adjustments Accounts, which are maintained under General Ledger:
    • In the Self Balancing Ledger system, three specific adjustment accounts are maintained to ensure that the ledgers are self-balancing.
    • The General Ledger Adjustment Account is created in the Debtors Ledger and Creditors Ledger to reflect the total balances of these ledgers in the General Ledger.
    • The Debtors or Sales Ledger Adjustment Account and Creditors or Purchase Ledger Adjustment Account are maintained in the General Ledger to reflect the balances of the Debtors Ledger and Creditors Ledger respectively.
    • This system helps in cross-verifying the balances and ensures accuracy in the accounting records.

Additional Information

  • Both statement - 1 and statement - 2 are incorrect:
    • This is incorrect because both statements accurately describe the workings of the Self Balancing Ledger system.
  • Only statement - 2 is correct:
    • This is incorrect because statement - 1 is also a correct description of the Self Balancing Ledger system.
  • Only statement - 1 is correct:
    • This is incorrect because statement - 2 is also a correct description of the Self Balancing Ledger system.

  • Direct payment by customer in Pass Book only:

    • However, if the Cash Book is not updated simultaneously, this amount will not appear in the Cash Book yet.
    • To reconcile the balances, this amount must be added to the Cash Book balance to match the Pass Book balance.

  • Cheques deposited in Bank, but not cleared:

  • Amount withdrawn from Bank not recorded in the Cash Book:
    • This option is incorrect. If an amount is withdrawn from the bank and not recorded in the Cash Book, it would actually decrease the bank balance, requiring a deduction rather than an addition.

questions.question: The main focus of _______ is on recording and classifying monetary transactions in the books of accounts and preparation of financial statements at the end of every accounting period.
questions.questionHtml: The main focus of _______ is on recording and classifying monetary transactions in the books of accounts and preparation of financial statements at the end of every accounting period.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is financial accounting.

Key Points

  • Financial Accounting:
    • Primarily concerned with the systematic recording, classifying, and summarizing of financial transactions.
    • Focuses on preparing financial statements, such as the income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement, which are used by external stakeholders including investors, creditors, and regulatory agencies.
    • Ensures that the financial information presented is accurate and in compliance with regulatory standards and accounting principles.
    • Helps stakeholders assess the financial health, performance, and changes in the financial position of an enterprise.

Additional Information

  • Environmental Accounting:
    • Focuses on accounting for environmental costs and benefits.
    • Involves the identification, measurement, and allocation of environmental costs, and the integration of these costs into business decisions and financial reports.
  • Forensic Accounting:
    • Specializes in investigating financial fraud and disputes.
    • Involves analyzing financial information to detect and prevent fraud and to support legal proceedings.
  • Cost Accounting:
    • Focuses on calculating and controlling costs associated with manufacturing or providing services.
    • Helps businesses in budgeting, cost control, and cost reduction strategies.

questions.question: Classify the following errors. (i) Credit sale of ₹1,500 to Piyush was correctly recorded in sales book but not posted to Piyush's Account. (ii) Purchases book was undercast by ₹100.
questions.questionHtml:
Classify the following errors.

(i) Credit sale of ₹1,500 to Piyush was correctly recorded in sales book but not posted to Piyush's Account.

(ii) Purchases book was undercast by ₹100.

options.text: (i) Errors of omission (ii) Errors of principle
(i) Errors of commission (ii) Errors of omission

options.text: (i) Errors of principle (ii) Errors of commission
options.html: (i) Errors of principle (ii) Errors of commission

options.text: (i) Errors of omission (ii) Errors of commission
options.html: (i) Errors of omission (ii) Errors of commission

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Errors of omission (i) and Errors of commission (ii).

Key Points

  • Credit sale of ₹1,500 to Piyush was correctly recorded in sales book but not posted to Piyush's Account:
    • This is an error of omission. The transaction was recorded in the sales book but was omitted from being posted to Piyush's account. Omissions can occur when a transaction is either completely or partially left out from the books of accounts.
    • In this case, the error is partial because the transaction was recorded in the sales book but not posted to the individual ledger account.
  • Purchases book was undercast by ₹100:
    • This is an error of commission. An error of commission occurs when an entry is made incorrectly, such as entering the wrong amount, wrong account, or wrong side of the account.
    • Undercasting the purchases book by ₹100 is an arithmetic error, which is a type of error of commission, where the total is calculated incorrectly.

Additional Information

  • Errors of principle:
    • These errors occur when accounting principles are not followed. For example, treating a capital expenditure as a revenue expenditure. None of the given errors fall under this category.
  • Errors of omission:
    • While (i) is correctly identified as an error of omission, (ii) is not. Errors of omission involve missing entries, either partially or completely, in the accounting records.
  • Errors of commission:
    • While (ii) is correctly identified as an error of commission, (i) is not. Errors of commission involve incorrect entries, such as wrong amounts or wrong accounts.
